style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare-transliteration in amp with Strong's carried in notes (matching the ch.1 pilot); em-dashes used sparingly.
chapterNote: Chapter 28 is a sustained meditation on righteousness and wickedness worked out in the public square -- in rulers, in commerce, in law, and in wealth. Two refrains frame it: the wicked who flee with no one chasing and hide when they rise to power (vv. 1, 12, 28), and the righteous who are bold as a lion and multiply when the wicked perish. Again and again the chapter sets the man who keeps the torah against the man who forsakes it (vv. 4, 7, 9), the honest poor against the crooked rich (vv. 6, 11, 20, 22), and the one who covers his sin against the one who confesses it (v. 13). The argument is that justice and prosperity are not finally secured by force or shrewd gain but by integrity before God -- a land flourishes under understanding and withers under oppression.

1.text: The wicked flee though no one gives chase, but the righteous are bold as a lion.
1.amp: The wicked [rasha -- the guilty, the criminal] flee [nus -- run, take flight] when no one pursues [radaph -- chases after], but the righteous [tsaddiq -- the just] are confident [batach -- secure, unafraid] as a lion.
1.notes: rasha (H7563) carries the guilt of one who has done wrong; guilt itself becomes the pursuer, so the wicked run from shadows (cf. Lev 26:17, 36). batach (H982) is the verb of settled trust -- the righteous man's courage is not nerve but the rest of a clear conscience before God.

2.text: When a land rebels, its rulers are many; but under a man of understanding and knowledge, order is kept and endures.
2.amp: For the transgression [pesha -- rebellion, revolt] of a land [eretz] its princes [sar -- rulers, officials] are many [rav]; but by a man [adam] of understanding [biyn -- discernment] and knowledge [yada], its right order [ken -- what is established, true] is prolonged [arak -- made to endure].
2.notes: pesha (H6588) is rebellion against rightful order; political churn -- rulers rising and falling in quick succession -- is read as the symptom of a land in revolt. By contrast one biyn-and-yada man (H995, H3045) can hold a nation steady, for stability flows from wisdom, not from a crowd of contenders.

3.text: A poor man who crushes the poor is like a driving rain that beats down the crops and leaves no bread.
3.amp: A poor [rush -- destitute] man [geber] who oppresses [ashaq -- exploits, extorts] the poor [dal -- the weak and lowly] is like a sweeping rain that leaves no food [lechem -- bread, grain].
3.notes: the bitterest oppression is the destitute (rush, H7326) turning on the equally destitute (dal, H1800) -- one who should be a brother becomes a flood. Rain ought to bring bread; this rain destroys it, the very thing meant to nourish becoming the agent of ruin.

4.text: Those who forsake the law praise the wicked, but those who keep it take their stand against them.
4.amp: Those who forsake [azab -- abandon] the law [torah -- instruction, teaching] praise [halal -- celebrate, applaud] the wicked [rasha]; but those who keep [shamar -- guard, observe] the law [torah] contend [garah -- stir themselves up, do battle] with them.
4.notes: torah (H8451) here is God's instruction as the dividing line: to abandon it is to end up cheering for evil, while to guard it puts a man at war (garah, H1624) with evildoers. There is no neutral ground -- the law forces a side.

5.text: Justice stays hidden from men bent on evil, but to all who search after the LORD its whole meaning lies open.
5.amp: Evil [ra] men [enosh -- mortals] do not understand [biyn -- discern, grasp] justice [mishpat -- right judgment]; but those who seek [baqash -- search after] the LORD [YHWH] understand [biyn] all things.
5.notes: mishpat (H4941) is the sense of what is right and just; the morally bent cannot even perceive it, their evil blinding their judgment. To seek the LORD (baqash, H1245) is the only door to true discernment -- knowledge of justice begins with knowledge of God (cf. 1:7; Jer 9:24).

6.text: Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than a rich man whose ways are crooked.
6.amp: Better [tov] is the poor [rush] who walks [halak] in his integrity [tom -- wholeness, blamelessness] than he who is crooked [iqqesh -- twisted, perverse] in his ways [derek], though he be rich [ashir].
6.notes: tom (H8537) is undivided wholeness, a life with no hidden seam (cf. 28:18; 19:1). The proverb overturns the world's scale of value: poverty with integrity outweighs wealth with a crooked walk, for a man's worth is measured by his way, not his portfolio.

7.text: Whoever guards the law is a discerning son, but a companion of gluttons brings shame to his father.
7.amp: Whoever keeps [natsar -- watches over, guards] the law [torah] is a son [ben] with understanding [biyn -- discernment]; but a companion [ra'ah -- one who runs with, keeps company] of gluttons shames [kalam -- disgraces, humiliates] his father [ab].
7.notes: natsar (H5341) is the careful, sentry-like guarding of the torah; the son who keeps it shows discernment, while the one who runs with the riotous (the margin reads 'feeds gluttons') drags his father into public disgrace. A son's company displays -- or betrays -- his upbringing (cf. 23:20-21).

8.text: Whoever swells his wealth by interest and extortion gathers it up for one who will be kind to the poor.
8.amp: He who increases [rabah -- multiplies] his substance [hon -- wealth, riches] by usury and unjust gain [tarbiyth -- excessive interest, increase] gathers [qabats -- collects, amasses] it for him who will show favor [chanan -- be gracious] to the poor [dal].
8.notes: tarbiyth (H8636) is exploitative interest, forbidden against the needy in Israel (Lev 25:36). By a quiet providence the hoard amassed on the backs of the poor is finally handed to the generous man who will spend it on them -- God reverses the flow (cf. 13:22; Job 27:16-17).

9.text: If a man turns a deaf ear to the law, even his prayer is detestable.
9.amp: He who turns away [sur -- removes, turns aside] his ear [ozen] from hearing [shama -- listening, heeding] the law [torah], even his prayer [tephillah] is an abomination [to'evah -- detestable, loathsome to God].
9.notes: shama (H8085) is hearing that obeys, not mere sound. The man who will not listen to God has no standing to ask anything of Him; his very prayer becomes to'evah (H8441), a thing God loathes -- obedience and access are bound together (cf. Ps 66:18; Isa 1:15; John 9:31).

10.text: Whoever leads the upright astray into an evil path will fall into his own pit, but the blameless will inherit good.
10.amp: Whoever causes the upright [yashar -- straight, righteous] to go astray [taah -- wander, be led off course] in an evil [ra] way [derek] will fall [naphal] into his own pit; but the blameless [tamim -- whole, without defect] will inherit [nachal -- take possession of] good [tov] things.
10.notes: the corrupter of the righteous digs his own grave -- the trap he sets springs back on him (cf. 26:27; Ps 7:15). nachal (H5157) is the inheritance verb, the language of receiving a lasting estate: the tamim (H8549) come into a good portion they did not seize but were given.

11.text: A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man with discernment sees right through him.
11.amp: The rich [ashir] man [ish] is wise [chakham -- skilled, shrewd] in his own eyes [ayin]; but the poor [dal] who has understanding [biyn -- discernment] searches him out [chaqar -- examines, sees through].
11.notes: wealth breeds self-flattery: the rich man mistakes his money for wisdom. chaqar (H2713) is to probe and investigate to the bottom; the discerning poor man, owing the rich nothing, sees past the facade to the real measure of the man (cf. 18:11; 26:16).

12.text: When the righteous triumph, there is great glory; but when the wicked rise to power, men go into hiding.
12.amp: When righteous [tsaddiq] men rejoice [alats -- exult, triumph], there is great [rav] glory [tipheret -- splendor, honor]; but when the wicked [rasha] rise [qum -- stand up, come to power], a man hides himself [chaphas -- conceals himself, is sought out].
12.notes: tipheret (H8597) is radiant public splendor -- a community visibly flourishes under righteous rule. When the wicked qum (H6965, rise to power), ordinary people vanish from sight, a refrain that bookends the chapter with v.1 and v.28: tyranny empties the public square of honest men.

13.text: He who hides his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and forsakes them will find mercy.
13.amp: He who covers [kasah -- conceals, hides] his sins [pesha -- transgressions] will not prosper [tsalach -- succeed, thrive]; but whoever confesses [yadah -- acknowledges, owns] and forsakes [azab -- abandons] them will obtain mercy [racham -- compassion].
13.notes: the great gospel proverb: concealment of sin chokes prosperity (cf. Ps 32:3-5), but yadah (H3034) -- to openly own one's guilt -- joined to azab (H5800), actually leaving it, opens the door to racham (H7355), God's tender mercy. Confession without forsaking is hollow; forsaking without confession is proud; both together find grace (cf. 1 John 1:9).

14.text: Blessed is the man who is always reverent, but whoever hardens his heart will fall into ruin.
14.amp: Happy [osher -- blessed, fortunate] is the man [adam] who fears [pachad -- trembles in awe] always [tamid -- continually]; but he who hardens [qashah -- stiffens, makes stubborn] his heart [leb] will fall [naphal] into trouble [ra -- calamity, evil].
14.notes: pachad (H6342) here is the reverent dread that keeps a man tender before God and watchful against sin -- a continual (tamid, H8548) holy caution, not anxious terror. Its opposite is the hardened heart (qashah, H7185), the calloused presumption that walks straight into ruin (cf. Phil 2:12; Heb 3:8).

15.text: Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a helpless people.
15.amp: As a roaring lion [aryeh] and a charging [shaqaq -- rushing, ranging hungrily] bear [dob], so is a wicked [rasha] ruler [mashal -- one who governs, has dominion] over the poor [dal] people [am -- the nation, the folk].
15.notes: the proverb strips the wicked ruler of every civilized pretense: he is simply a predator, lion and bear in one, and the dal (H1800) are his prey. shaqaq (H8264) suggests the restless, ravenous prowling of a beast that has not eaten -- power without righteousness is appetite armed with a throne (cf. 28:3; Ezek 22:27).

16.text: A ruler who lacks understanding is a cruel oppressor, but he who hates unjust gain will lengthen his days.
16.amp: The prince [nagid -- leader, ruler] who lacks understanding [tebunah -- discernment, intelligence] is also a great [rav] oppressor [maatsoth -- extortioner]; but he who hates [sane] unjust gain [betsa -- profit gotten by violence or fraud] will prolong [arak -- lengthen] his days [yom].
16.notes: betsa (H1215) is the cut of profit grasped at any cost -- the master sin already named in 1:19. A ruler without tebunah (H8394) inevitably turns oppressor, for only discernment restrains power; but the leader who hates ill-gotten gain secures long days, since righteousness, not plunder, is what truly establishes a throne (cf. 16:12; 29:14).

17.text: A man weighed down by the guilt of bloodshed will be a fugitive to the grave; let no one hold him back.
17.amp: A man [adam] burdened by the blood [dam] of any person [nephesh -- a human life, a soul] will flee [nus -- run, take flight] to the pit [bor -- the grave, the dungeon]; let no one support [tamak -- hold up, uphold] him.
17.notes: the murderer is haunted to his grave (bor, H953) by the blood-guilt he bears; tamak (H8551) is to lay hold of and uphold. The wisdom here is sobering: do not shield or shore up the one whose hands are stained with innocent blood, for justice must run its course (cf. Gen 9:6; Num 35:33).

18.text: Whoever walks blamelessly will be kept safe, but the man of crooked ways will fall all at once.
18.amp: Whoever walks [halak] uprightly [tamim -- whole, blameless] will be saved [yasha -- delivered, kept safe]; but he who is perverse [iqqesh -- twisted, crooked] in his ways [derek] will fall [naphal] suddenly [echad -- in a single moment, all at once].
18.notes: the contrast is between the tamim (H8549), whose wholeness keeps him standing, and the iqqesh (H6140), whose double, crooked way finally gives out beneath him. echad (H259), 'in one,' pictures a fall that is sudden and total -- the crooked man's ruin comes in a single instant, with no slow warning (cf. 28:10).

19.text: Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but whoever chases empty schemes will have his fill of poverty.
19.amp: He who tills [abad -- works, labors over] his land [adamah -- the ground, the soil] will have plenty [sabah -- be satisfied, filled] of bread [lechem]; but he who follows [radaph -- pursues, chases] vain [req -- empty, worthless] pursuits will have his fill of poverty.
19.notes: abad (H5647) is patient, ordinary labor on the soil -- the unglamorous path to a full table. radaph (H7291), to chase after empty things (req, H7386), is the same verb that hunted no one in v.1: here it hunts illusions. The proverb blesses faithful work over get-rich fantasy (cf. 12:11; 14:23).

20.text: A faithful man will overflow with blessings, but whoever rushes to get rich will not go unpunished.
20.amp: A faithful [emunah -- trustworthy, steadfast] man [ish] will abound [rav -- be great, many] with blessings [berakah]; but he who hastens [uts -- presses, rushes] to be rich [ashar] will not be held innocent [naqah -- go unpunished, be acquitted].
20.notes: emunah (H530) is steady faithfulness -- reliability over time -- and it draws blessing as surely as the frantic rush for wealth (uts, H213) draws guilt. The issue is not riches but the haste: the man who must be rich now will cut the corners that leave him guilty (naqah, H5352) before God (cf. 28:22; 13:11; 1 Tim 6:9).

21.text: To show partiality is not good, yet for a mere crust of bread a man will do wrong.
21.amp: To have respect of persons [nakar -- to regard the face, to favor by appearance] is not good [tov]; yet for a piece of bread [lechem] a man [geber] will transgress [pasha -- rebel, sin willfully].
21.notes: to judge by the panim, the face -- the rank or wealth of the man before you -- corrupts justice (cf. Deut 1:17). The shock of the proverb is how cheaply integrity is sold: not for a fortune but for a crust, a man will pasha (H6586), deliberately do wrong. Small bribes corrupt as surely as large ones.

22.text: A stingy man scrambles after wealth and never knows that want is on its way to him.
22.amp: He [ish] who hastens [bahal -- is driven, frantic] after riches [hon -- wealth] has an evil [ra] eye [ayin], and does not know [yada] that poverty [cheser -- want, lack] will come [bo -- overtake] upon him.
22.notes: the 'evil eye' (ra ayin) is the grasping, grudging glance of the stingy and greedy (cf. 23:6; Matt 20:15). bahal (H926) is to act in driven haste; the irony is that the very poverty he dreads is bearing down on him precisely because of his frantic, joyless greed -- he chases wealth and outruns it into want.

23.text: Whoever rebukes a man will in the end find more favor than the one who flatters with his tongue.
23.amp: He who rebukes [yakach -- reproves, corrects] a man [adam] afterward [achar -- in the end, later] will find [matsa] more favor [chen -- grace, goodwill] than he who flatters [chalaq -- makes smooth, speaks slippery words] with the tongue [lashon].
23.notes: yakach (H3198) is honest, corrective confrontation -- painful in the moment but proven loving over time. chalaq (H2505) is to make the tongue smooth and slippery, the flatterer's art. The proverb measures by the end (achar, H310): truth that wounds wins the lasting gratitude that flattery never earns (cf. 27:5-6; 29:5).

24.text: Whoever robs his father or mother and says, 'It is no sin,' is a partner to the destroyer.
24.amp: Whoever robs [gazal -- seizes, takes by violent force] his father [ab] or his mother [em], and says, 'It is no transgression [pesha],' the same is a companion [chaver -- partner, associate] of a destroyer [shachath -- one who ruins, corrupts].
24.notes: gazal (H1497) is violent plunder, not quiet borrowing; to strip one's own parents and then deny the wrong (pesha) is to silence conscience itself. Such a self-justifying thief is chaver (H2270) -- bound in fellowship -- with the shachath (H7843), the destroyer; defrauding family is no lesser crime dressed up, but partnership in ruin (cf. 19:26; Mark 7:11-13).

25.text: A greedy heart stirs up strife, but whoever trusts in the LORD will be enriched.
25.amp: He who is of a proud, greedy [rachab -- wide, broad of appetite] heart [nephesh -- soul, desire] stirs up [garah -- provokes, foments] strife [madon -- contention, quarreling]; but he who trusts [batach -- relies, rests] in the LORD [YHWH] will be made fat [dashen -- prosper, be enriched].
25.notes: rachab nephesh, literally a 'wide soul,' is the swollen, insatiable appetite that grabs more and so breeds quarrels (garah, H1624). Against grasping stands batach (H982), restful trust in the LORD; the man who does not have to seize for himself is the one God makes prosper (dashen, H1878) -- a striking reversal of how greed thinks wealth is won.

26.text: Whoever trusts in his own heart is a fool, but whoever walks in wisdom will be kept safe.
26.amp: He who trusts [batach] in his own heart [leb] is a fool [kesil -- a dullard, the thick-headed]; but whoever walks [halak] in wisdom [chokmah], he will be delivered [malat -- escape, be rescued].
26.notes: the same trust-verb (batach, H982) of v.25 is here aimed wrongly: to rest in one's own heart -- self-confident, unexamined -- is the mark of the kesil (H3684). True security comes not from following the heart but from walking in chokmah, wisdom outside oneself; the one who does is delivered (malat, H4422) from the snares the self-trusting fool walks straight into (cf. 3:5-7; Jer 17:9).

27.text: Whoever gives to the poor will lack nothing, but whoever shuts his eyes to them will gather many curses.
27.amp: He who gives [natan -- bestows, grants] to the poor [rush -- the destitute] will not lack [machsor -- be in want]; but he who hides [alam -- conceals, looks away] his eyes [ayin] will have many [rav] a curse [meerah -- curse, calamity].
27.notes: open hands meet no want -- generosity to the rush (H7326) is met by God's provision, so the giver never falls short (cf. 11:24-25; 19:17). To 'hide the eyes' (alam, H5956) is the deliberate refusal to see the needy; that calculated blindness draws down many a curse, both the cry of the wronged poor and the judgment of the God who sees them.

28.text: When the wicked rise to power, men go into hiding; but when they perish, the righteous flourish.
28.amp: When the wicked [rasha] rise [qum -- stand up, come to power], men [adam] hide [satar -- conceal] themselves; but when they perish [abad -- are destroyed, vanish], the righteous [tsaddiq] increase [rabah -- multiply, flourish].
28.notes: the chapter closes by returning to its opening refrain (vv. 1, 12): under the wicked's rise, honest men go into hiding (satar, H5641); when the wicked perish (abad, H6), the righteous multiply (rabah, H7235) and the public square fills again. Tyranny suppresses; its fall lets righteousness flourish -- a quiet confidence that wicked power is never the last word (cf. 11:10; 29:2).
